stages.name: Observe
stages.instruction: Move the $R$ and $C$ sliders. Watch the Bode magnitude curve on the right shift left/right. The purple marker sits on the cutoff frequency $f_c$ (where $|H| = -3\,\text{dB}$). Below $f_c$ the filter passes; above, it attenuates at $-20\,\text{dB/décade}$. Advance after visiting at least $3$ different $f_c$ decades.
stages.concept: A first-order RC low-pass has transfer function $|H(f)| = 1 / \sqrt{1 + (f/f_c)^2}$, with cutoff $f_c = 1/(2\pi\,R\,C)$. In decibels: $|H|_{\text{dB}} = -10\,\log_{10}\!\bigl(1 + (f/f_c)^2\bigr)$. The gain is $\approx 0\,\text{dB}$ (flat) far below $f_c$, drops by $3\,\text{dB}$ at $f_c$, then falls linearly on the log-log plot with slope $-20\,\text{dB/décade}$ above $f_c$.

stages.name: Experiment
stages.instruction: Adjust $R$ and $C$ to place the cutoff at the target frequency shown by the dashed orange line ($f_c = 1\,\text{kHz}$). Many $(R, C)$ pairs work — you just need $R\,C = 1/(2\pi\,f_c)$.
stages.concept: Design formula: $f_c = 1/(2\pi\,R\,C)$, so $R\,C = 1/(2\pi\,f_c)$. For $f_c = 1000\,\text{Hz}$ you need $R\,C \approx 1.59\times10^{-4}\,\text{s}$ ($159\,\mu\text{s}$). Example combinations: $R = 1.59\,\text{k}\Omega$ with $C = 100\,\text{nF}$, or $R = 15.9\,\text{k}\Omega$ with $C = 10\,\text{nF}$. What matters is the product, not the individual values.

stages.name: Evaluate
stages.instruction: Component values are hidden. Read $f_c$ directly from the Bode magnitude curve — it's the frequency where $|H|$ crosses $-3\,\text{dB}$, or equivalently the corner where the flat region meets the $-20\,\text{dB/décade}$ slope.
stages.concept: Reading $f_c$ off a Bode plot: find where the curve is $3\,\text{dB}$ below the DC gain (the $-3\,\text{dB}$ horizontal line is drawn). Alternatively, the intersection of the two asymptotes (flat top-line and sloping side-line) is exactly $f_c$. Both methods give the same answer.

labels.question: question
labels.evaluate_prompt: The component values are hidden. Read the cutoff frequency f_c from the Bode plot alone.
labels.tip1: R↑ or C↑ → f_c shifts left ; f_c = 1/(2π·R·C)
labels.tip2: adjust R·C until the purple marker sits on the orange line
labels.tip3: read f_c off the plot where |H| = −3 dB

1.1: The purple dot on the plot marks f_c. Try increasing R and watch it shift.
1.2: f_c = 1/(2π·R·C). If you double R, f_c halves. If you halve C, f_c doubles.
1.3: You need to visit 3 different decades of f_c. Try R = 100 Ω with small C, then large C, then large R.

2.1: You need R·C = 1/(2π·1000) ≈ 1.59×10⁻⁴ s. Pick round C then compute R.
2.3: Or try C = 10 nF and R = 16 kΩ. Or C = 1 µF and R = 160 Ω. All give f_c = 1 kHz.

3.1: Look at where the curve crosses the horizontal −3 dB line (the orange dashed line).
3.2: Or find the 'knee' — where the flat part turns into the sloped part. That corner is f_c.
3.3: Read the x-axis at that point. Remember it's a log scale: each major tick is a factor of 10.
